subsubtopic: EFFICACY OF 1971 TAX LEGISLATION IN RELIEVING BURDEN ON LOW INCOME CANADIANS-FURTHER MEASURES TO PROVIDE EQUITY

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
That this House regrets the failure of the government to develop policies to create and operate Crown corporations for the benefit of the public, and condemns the government for divesting itself of its holdings and giving preferential treatment to private corporations in the field of public transportation to the detriment of corporations which belong to the people of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the course of the years, this country, whatever may have been the government of the day, has found it necessary in some areas to establish publicly owned industries for the benefit of all the people of Canada. We are raising the subject today because there are ominous signs that successful Crown corporations are being dismantled or deliberately hobbled in respect of their further development. I want to emphasize that I am not placing this motion before the House in any doctrinaire sense or along doctrinaire lines, but because what is happening now to Air Canada and other corporations threatens to distort the development of the Canadian economy in key areas. That is the only reason we raise the matter today.
I wish to deal first with Air Canada. I want to address my remarks particularly to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), if he will do me the honour of paying attention to what I say. Someone had better poke him in the ribs. Perhaps the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) could do that. I say to the Minister of Transport that what his department is doing to Air Canada and the preferences it is giving to CP Air are a scandal and a disservice to the people of Canada as well as to the future of the publicly-owned airline.
March 23, 1973

I refer first to the fact that he gave the route to Peking to CP Air. I heard someone on the other side say to me the other day that Air Canada was not particularly anxious to get the route to Peking. Let me inform the Minister of Transport that I have spoken to chief executives of Air Canada who have emphatically stated that they wanted and needed the route to Peking. They realized it might have been a losing route for a few years, which is always the case in such development, but they recognize that China and the area around it is an important area of growth, so for Air Canada that route would eventually have become a very important and profitable operation.
But what disturbs me more than I can say is that for a long time now the department has had before it the question of which one of Canada's carriers will be landing in Milan, Italy. I am worried about the length of time which the department is taking in making that decision, because it seems to me obvious that it ought to go without question to Air Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
I say to the minister that if he yields to the advice he may be receiving from the privately oriented mandarins in his department and gives the route to Milan to CP Air, that will be a further betrayal of the importance of Air Canada and of its future as a publicly owned airline. The argument is made-at least I have heard it- that to give Air Canada Milan while CP Air has Rome, would create competition between those two airlines in the same country. May I remind the minister and members of the House that CP Air was given Amsterdam in a context to which I will refer in a minute, and although Amsterdam is in a different country from Brussels, or some other very close airport, the fact is that that is competition even closer to Air Canada competition than Milan would be to Rome.
What has happened in the history of our airlines in Canada is to me very significant and very revealing about both old parties in this blessed and great country of ours. We had established a publicly owned airline in line with most countries in the world. There are very few countries which have privately owned airlines, the biggest one among them being the United States. We have followed the Americans in many areas, not all of them beneficial to Canada may I underline.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: I wish the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who eats private enterprise for breakfast, regurgitates it at lunch, and does something even less elegant with it at dinnertime, would hold his seat, Mr. Speaker, and not jump every time we talk about a publicly owned airline.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Your stuff is so sanctimonious anyway.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
The thing is, we had a publicly owned airline which the people of Canada established as air transportation became of some importance. Then, the Conservative government in 1959 started the ball rolling for the private-
Crown Corporations
ly owned CP Air. It said to CP Air that it could have one or more airports in Canada, transcontinental routes. Then, in 1966 or 1967, the then minister of transport, the hon. Mr. Pickersgill, who did a great deal of good for Canada in that department, as he told me, but no matter how carefully I have looked I have not yet been able to find it, decided on a policy of dividing the world. Let us look at this policy and see how indefendable it is.
How did they divide the world between the two airlines? They gave Air Canada northern Europe-that is how Air Canada got Moscow-including the United Kingdom, and the Caribbean, and they allotted to CP Air southern Europe, the growing Pacific area, Mexico and Latin America. That was supposed to be an equal division. To me, it looks more like a rabbit and a horse. CP Air received all the growing areas of the world, with the exception of Africa which has not yet entered the picture. They have the whole of the Asian continent, which is growing and will be an important source for air transportation passengers and cargo, all of Latin America, which will be an important source also. Mexico is already a most profitable source of revenue for CP Air which at first got Mexico city and now has two or three more airports in Mexico. Air Canada cannot go there, yet Mexico is an important tourist country to which many Canadians go at different times in the year.
This scandalous division of the world is now being kept, and if the department continues along this course, CP Air will be the most powerful and most profitable Canadian air carrier while our own carrier, which is owned by the people of Canada, will have its growth stunted. What sense is there in that? Perhaps the ladies and gentlemen in the House may know that every time I think of CP Air I get a little apoplectic. We built the goldarned company with people's money, with people's land. They now have a huge empire, and as if that were not enough, when they are in competition with the publicly owned airline, we want to make certain that this large economic empire will have the opportunity for growth, development and profits while we stunt our own airline.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
That is totally indefensible. I hope that the present Minister of Transport is differently oriented from my friend, Mr. Pickersgill. I have said some unkind things about some other friends I had in the Bank of Canada whom I appear to have lost. I do not know whether Mr. Pickersgill will continue to be my friend. I certainly know that Mr. Pickersgill did a disservice to Canada in this policy which he established, and I also know that as chairman of the CTC, he did not do service to Canada by the way in which Bell Telephone got away with whatever it wanted and by the way in which the railways got away with whatever they wanted in rail line abandonment and everything that is contrary to the needs of the Canadian people. I know that the present Minister of Transport used to have a different kind of orientation and I think he still does. I appeal to him to stop this indefensible, conscienceless bending before CP Air and Canadian Pacific and give our own airline the opportunity which it ought to have for future growth and development in an era when transport is becoming daily more important for all the people of Canada.

March 23, 1973
Crown Corporations

speechtext: They had better improve their service to Ottawa.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Here we go. Those are the usual stories. I have been on CP Air when I could not use Air Canada. I have been on CP Air and I say to these gentleman, and to their friends whose corporate rip-off they are determined to support no matter what their political position may be, that Air Canada is every bit as good as CP Air, if not better-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: -except that it is an airline owned by the people of Canada. Therefore, when it progresses, makes profits and has a surplus, it does so on behalf of the people of Canada, whereas CP Air's profits and surpluses are on behalf of the rich, investors of Canadian Pacific. God alone knows they have taken enough out of the flesh of the Canadian people, and they are not entitled to any more.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
It is really interesting to note some of the directors of CP Air. We have President Ian Sinclair, who is the head of it. They are little people, Mr. Speaker. You have always to remember that the directors of these large economic corporations are modest Canadians like Thomas Bata, the head of Bata shoes; Charles Bronfman, one of the heads of the liquor interests in this country; Hon. E. C. Manning, the modest ex-Premier of Alberta, and H. A. Martin, who is also at the same time a director of the Canada Development Corporation.
When you look at other subsidiaries of Canadian Pacific you find such little people as Duff Roblin, who is President of CP Investments, and J. V. Clyne, a Macmillan-Blo-edell executive; W. Earle McLaughlin, the unknown head of the Royal Bank and a director of the Power Corporation of Canada. These are the people who already have directorships in every important industry in this country, and have their hands on every important economic lever in this country. It is to these people that the ministry of transport hands over the best opportunities for development, from the point of view of the future, at the expense of Air Canada and the people of this country. If there are members of this House who are not eaten up by doctrinaire love for so-called private enterprise, which is not private at all any more, then they ought to tell the Minister of Transport that this parliament will not stand for any more erosion of the future prospects of the people's airline of this country.
At the same time, look at what has happened with the Canadian Development Corporation. That was, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, a valuable idea, an idea which, as we have pointed out to parliament on a number of occasions, our party suggested at its founding convention in 1961. We called it a Canadian Development Fund at that time. It was an idea for garnering large amounts of capital for investment so as to make sure that Canadian development is in Canadian hands, and that areas in Canada which cannot attract private capital will have a source of funds for their development. Its purpose as well was to make

sure that developments in new areas, in electronics and other new technology and scientific development in this country will not be in the hands of foreign corporations, or even of domestic private corporations, but will be in the hands of the people of Canada through some appropriate organizations.
One of my colleagues, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight), will deal with this subject in greater detail later today, but I want to deal with it as a whole for a moment. This was a good idea, an important idea for a country like Canada. It was an important idea for two very significant reasons. One is the extent to which our economy is now owned and controlled from outside. It was necessary to make certain that such a fund of investment capital was not in the hands of private investors who would just as soon, or sooner, sell to an American corporation for a fast buck than be concerned with Canada's economic independence. It was, therefore, important to have a publicly-managed fund of investment capital available for the purpose of retaining, at least in the future, the economic development of this country in Canadian hands. There is only one guaranteed way that anything will remain in Canadian hands, and that is if it is in the hands of the people of Canada instead of in the hands of a private corporation.
The second reason that was an important idea was that this country, like many countries in the world, has large underdeveloped areas that cannot be a place for private investment without public assistance. Those areas have never been profitable for private enterprise and are not likely ever to be profitable for private enterprise. That is recognized in the Department of Regional Economic Expansion where, in a way that I do not agree with but at least it underlines what I am saying, that department spends hundreds of millions of dollars of the people's money to build industry in these disadvantaged areas, so that even this government now recognizes these areas cannot develop without public intervention.
This was the other idea behind the Canadian Development Fund which we proposed in 1961. This was an important idea, and important for significant reasons. But what has happened to the Canada Development Corporation, as we foretold at the time would happen, and which was the reason we opposed it and why we moved numerous amendments which were defeated both by the Tories and Liberals in this House, is that it has become a mutual investment fund that takes no account at all of the needs in Canada, that does not appear to be concerned in the slightest with economic development in this country, and that is interested only in making itself into some kind of profitable organization. What other reason could there be for putting its hands on Polymer? In God's name, what other reason could there be for that? Here was an organization set up during the Second World War which has served Canada well, which has been a profitable undertaking, and which has operations outside Canada even now. What reason was there for the Canada Development Corporation to lay its hands on it, except that here was a profitable organization that it wanted to make part of its profit-seeking self?
The Canada Development Corporation has gone into partnership with Venturetek and West Venture-I think
March 23, 1973

that is its name, a similar operation on the west coast. The president of Venturetek is the son of a board member of the Canada Development Corporation, who himself had been head of that same corporation earlier, I think just before he became a member of the board of CDC. And I am informed that the west coast, so-called Venture organization, has hardly had any money put into it by private people. But now they will get part of the profits, if profits there be.
Of what value is this mutual investment fund now? A great important idea for the development of Canada in Canadian hands has been distorted and destroyed by the government, with the assistance and support of the Tory opposition, until it has been turned into a mutual investment fund that serves no purpose other than to try to attach existing investment corporations of this country. Indeed, Sir, the CDC-

He wanted to be certain that everything was held for his friends in Calgary and Edmonton, as if they did not already have enough of Canada and Canada's resources.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has something important to say I am sure.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been listening very carefully, as I usually do, to the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis). From what he has said it seemed that he was condemning the sale of Polymer to the Canadian Development Corporation. Do I understand that he actually condemns that sale?'

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member understands correctly. I condemn that sale-I condemn that sale with all the vigour I have. There was no excuse for it and there is no logic in CDC doing that. There is no good economic reason and I condemn it, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian Development Corporation has $250 million of the people's money to invest and I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is a waste of that money merely to buy up something that already functions efficiently. That is not
Crown Corporations
using the money properly and the government ought to tell the CDC to cut it out.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) ought to be ashamed of having agreed to the sale of Polymer to CDC. I ask him in all seriousness, what value there is in taking $60-odd million or $70-odd million of the $250 million capital of public money given to the CDC and using it to buy Polymer, an existing corporation, what addition to Canada's wealth does that represent? If that $60 million or $70 million had been used to set up some industry in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Northern Ontario, Saskatchewan, or Quebec, there would have been an addition to the wealth of the country and additional opportunities for jobs for Canadian workers. This action of the CDC is a shameful grabbing along the lines of the usual economic empires which now throttle Canada and should not be permitted.
The CDC has become an extension of Power Corporation of Canada, which I find to be a nest of Liberal birds-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Vultures.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
-or probably vultures, Mr. Speaker. There are people representing Power Corporation or who were earlier associated with it on the board of directors of CDC still acting in the only way they know; they never think in terms of the needs of the people or the needs of the country but think as directors of whichever corporations they headed in private enterprise. This is the kind of distortion which has been made of a good idea, Mr. Speaker.
The idea of CDC taking over Eldorado and the 45 per cent that the government of Canada owns in Panarctic is * a shuddering distortion of the needs in this country. The money is being used to take over existing situations without adding to the wealth of the country. It is asking that the government should consider selling the 45 per cent of Panarctic which ought to be at least 51 per cent because this parliament, not the private consortiums, ought to have a controlling interest in that Panarctic and the developments of Northern Canada. If there is wealth in the north it ought to be exploited on behalf of the people of Canada, not on behalf of the private corporations. Only if it is exploited that way will there be some concern with the rights of the native people and the environment of that area.
I want to underline, Mr. Speaker, that it is significant that they should even consider it because, if there is another area of probable growth in the future and probable profitability in the future, instead of coming back into the Treasury of Canada to be used for various programs on behalf of the people of Canada it will be added to the profits to attract investors in what is now a mutual investment fund.
As I have already said, Mr. Speaker, one of my colleagues will deal with the CDC in detail and another will deal with Polymer in detail. I want to conclude on this point, if I may. My colleagues and I do not claim that other members of this parliament and people who do not support us in Canada are any less concerned about the future of the country than we. I do say, however, Mr. Speaker, that there is a feeling in the youth of Canada

March 23, 1973
Crown Corporations
which parliament ought to share, that this country is being handed over recklessly.
I had the honour of being invited last night by the Student Council of the University of Western Ontario to participate in an exercise which they called "Confidence Canada." The well-known writer and broadcaster, Pierre Berton, and I were honoured in being invited to receive awards from the Student Council in relation to Canadian independence, both economic and cultural. I do not know exactly how many people were there, but I was told that the hall holds more than 2,000 people and it appeared to be full. That is not as important as the fact that the young people, at least 90 per cent of the audience, consisted of university students and some upper grade high school students. That audience of more than 2,000 young Canadians was enthusiastic about this country. The propositions which we put to them about the need for regaining control of Canada's economy and developing a Canadian culture of independence, beauty and strength, was received with warmth and enthusiasm. I told them at the end of the meeting that they moved and inspired me much more than I could possibly have hoped to move and inspire them.
Mr. Speaker, across this country there is a growing appreciation of the fact that our wealth is being exploited for private gain and not for public good; it is being exploited mainly for the gain of large multinational corporations and not for the objectives of this country. There is a growing realization of that and there is a growing demand that the sellout of Canada should stop, and that the riches that this country has be developed in this country for the welfare of its people and, in so far as we can %pare them, for the welfare of other peoples in the world who need them and not for those who are already rich and powerful.
What we are saying in this motion is that development of this country requires more and more public involvement and public investment. We are saying that the policies with regard to Air Canada, to the Canadian Development Corporation, to Polymer and to Panarctic on which . this government is now embarked is a reversal of progress in this country and must stop. We hope that this government will be persuaded to stop it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say at the outset that it is not very often I have the opportunity of following the distinguished member for York South (Mr. Lewis), who always speaks with such eloquence and conviction. We heard again today his usual rhetoric and his exposition of socialist philosophy. He seems to speak with more determination and conviction each day. It seems to me that power has gone to his head. He would sooner promote his own philosophy than meet the challenges inherent in any action that is necessary to meet the transportation needs of the Canadian people. It is obvious, from the drafting of the motion, that he is concerned about the government's failure to develop policies relating to corporations which belong to the people of Canada; yet he did not say anything about the need for improving the transportation network in Canada and overcoming some of the deficiencies. I hope that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), to whom the hon. member addressed a good portion of his speech, will not

be overly concerned with the appraoch taken by the hon. member for York South who preceded me.
Let me give a good example of how a private regional air carrier moved into a vacuum which was left by Air Canada. I am speaking about the service between Edmonton and Calgary. Some years ago, Air Canada gave up the route between Edmonton and Calgary because it was losing money. Pacific Western took on that route and provided an air bus service. On week days there are six flights each way between Calgary and Edmonton. You can fly from Calgary to Edmonton in 35 minutes. There is no waiting time. You walk into the air terminal, buy your ticket, get on the aircraft, and you can travel from Edmonton to Calgary in less than one hour, travelling time to and from the airport included. This has been a very successful venture.
One might ask this question: If that service is so successful and efficient between Edmonton and Calgary, why is it not feasible to set up the same kind of service to serve Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal?
The leader of the NDP referred to the awarding of the route to Milan. I, too, wish that the government would make a decision about the awarding of this particular route, because it seems to me that the delay will only add further confusion and frustration for the air carrier who will eventually be awarded it. It will make it more difficult for that air carrier to capitalize on the summer travel season this year, which will be the annual peak. I hope the government, in making any decision, will not be dictated to, and I hope it will not listen to any threats made by the President of Air Canada, Mr. Pratt, who has suggested that he would quit in disgust if the route is not awarded to Air Canada.
If the government awards that route to Air Canada, it must clarify its policy. Aviation policy was defined in 1965, and under it CP Air was designated to serve the whole Pacific area, including the whole of Asia, Australia, New Zealand, as well as southern and southeastern Europe and Latin America. Air Canada was designated to serve Britain, western, northern and eastern Europe, and the Caribbean, with this exception: CP Air was to continue to serve the Netherlands through Amsterdam. It seems to me that under established policy CP Air should rightfully be awarded access to this route, and I think the government owes it to the House to explain its new policy if it is contemplating a deviation from the existing policy.
When we look at the needs which confront us in transportation in this country, in the air, on land and on water, it will be seen, I think, that there is a need for both private and public investment if we are to be successful in developing a co-ordinated and integrated transport system in this country. Those of us who travel on the airlines know that competition is needed if we are to be given the kind of service to which people are entitled. Certainly, the federal government should encourage a great deal more research into many modes of transportation. I believe there is a great deal of work to be done on tracked air cushioned vehicles and intercity rapid transit. I believe those avenues should be explored. While this is being
March 23, 1973

done, it would be wise to improve and polish some of the facilities which we now possess.
The Canadian Transport Commission Research Branch, in its Intercity Passenger Transport Study of September, 1970, said in part:
-in the 1970's the greatest benefit would be derived from improvements in the existing modes, such as on-time reliability (and consequent reduction in waiting times), passenger processing procedures, and rail improvements using existing trackage.
-access to terminals and processing waiting times in terminals make up a large segment of total trip time and consequently improvements in this area will have significant payoffs.
The travelling public is not so much concerned with the amount of time that is spent in the air as with the frustration and confusion that is created on the ground. I am speaking of methods of handling passengers, of luggage handling methods and of how tickets are processed. The CNR, for example, is a Crown corporation, but I do not think it is a leader or an innovator in this field. I believe that the corporation should be addressing itself to shortcomings in these areas. Advances and improvements in rail passenger service have been few in the past years. I suggest that all this is not only a challenge to the private sector, but a challenge to the public sector as well, including existing Crown corporations. My main concern has not to do with the effect which private enterprise will have on government sponsored bodies. My biggest concern is to see that the Canadian public is given the kind of service it is entitled to, at reasonable prices. My remarks also apply to the transportation of goods.
There was a debate on Tuesday in which it was pointed out by many in this House that inequities and discriminations in the application of railway freight rates have had an unfortunate effect on the various regions of this country. It is imperative that we develop an effective and equitable freight rate structure which will apply to the transportation of goods from region to region. That structure must not work to the detriment of any region of Canada, particularly the Atlantic region and the western region. The CNR is more concerned about sprucing up its corporate image than addressing itself to the needs of transportation. Double page ads in the major magazines throughout Canada do not really refer to transportation, but real estate investment. I have here a double page ad which indicates the huge tracts of land they are utilizing to erect buildings and shopping centres. I notice that even the town of Vegreville is included in this particular ad.
There is an ad in Time magazine which boasts about the CNR operating so efficiently year after year. It asks "Why don't we end up in the black more often?" There are a lot of Canadians asking the same question. Rather than the CNR concerning itself with a public relations campaign, it would do much better to take a look at its rail passenger service and spruce it up a little so that Canadians who are desirous of travelling by rail will have the opportunity to do so comfortably and efficiently.
There is no question that we need improvements in our air service in this country. We have two major air carriers which basically provide trans-continental and international service. These airlines could be complemented to a much greater degree by an effective co-ordinated regional
Crown Corporations
air carrier policy. This whole system should devote itself to serving the passenger needs of all of Canada and particular regions, not when it suits the carrier but when it suits the passenger.
There are a number of regional air carriers in Canada which have done a very good job. However, a clear cut air transportation policy utilizing the two major air carriers, co-ordinated by the regional air carriers, is something we need in this country. Pacific Western Airlines, which filled a vacuum in the western part of Canada, Eastern Pacific Airlines and Transair are indeed carriers that we need in this country. They are efficient and effective. I do not believe they would do a better job if they were nationalized.
There is a lot of talk about the service received from Air Canada, particularly as it relates to western points. Some of the services leave much to be desired. The service between Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal is such that on any given day it is difficult to get a reservation to travel from city to city. If you do not book your flight a week in advance, you will be flying by the seat of your pants. If this national air carrier cannot put on more aircraft to supply the needs of the people, someone else should be allowed to do it.

You cannot have a monopoly and fail to provide the service which the public needs. Pacific Western Airlines, which serves the cities of Calgary and Edmonton, have filled the void created by Air Canada which felt it was not economical to serve those two cities. This is a profitable operation and renders the kind of service that is needed between those two cities. The carrier is happy and the public are happy.
The frustrations of passengers wanting to fly between Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal is obvious. I have experienced it many times. When I journey westward to Edmonton on a weekend, I must stop off in Toronto. I have waited as long as 10 hours to get my connecting flight. Flight 137 which travels from Saint John to Toronto and on to Edmonton has never been on time on a Friday night for the past two months. These are some of the things which frustrate Canadians.
The airlines and the passengers, particularly the passengers, find that Toronto is a huge bottleneck when travelling to Ottawa. Also, the citizens of Toronto do not appreciate having these extra flights around their city. Why can we not have a direct air link between the capital city of Canada and the capital city of Alberta? Surely, the city of Edmonton has matured to the stage where it deserves a direct link by Canada's national air carrier. You either have to go to Winnipeg and wait for an hour and a half or go to Toronto and wait for an hour and a half. There is a not a direct link by Canada's national airline between the city of Ottawa and the city of Calgary. There again there are stopovers, delays, frustrations and traffic jams in Toronto or an undue wait in Winnipeg.
There is something else that is needed in Alberta. It is high time the city of Edmonton was awarded a bilateral service to the United States. Edmonton is the only city in Canada that does not have a direct link to the United States. Bilateral talks have been going on, but nothing has

developed. They have been stalled. We would like to know what the future holds with respect to this application. I have a letter from the Edmonton Business Development Department which puts forth in a nutshell the reasons and the desirability for Edmonton gaining this access. I quote:

Therefore, it is vital that Edmonton obtain the route from Twin Cities (Winnipeg), Edmonton-Anchorage daily jet service. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I also wish to thank the hon. members who have given me this opportunity to conclude my remarks. I reiterate the necessity of upgrading and improving air transportation service, particularly as it relates to western Canada. I also point out at this time that parliament has not had an opportunity of examining the 1971 annual report of Air Canada. I believe there are many areas both the committee and parliament could explore. Many questions remain to be answered, particularly those related to its sales and promotional charges.
I should like also to point out that the approach indicated in the recent policy enunciated by the minister respecting northern development and transportation by land, air and sea is sadly lacking in imagination, particularly with regard to air transport. I believe the policy blatantly disregards the relationship of the province of Alberta to the development of a uniform and effective northwestern transportation policy. The plan advances seven key recommendations. I believe that to disregard the province of Alberta, particularly the city of Edmonton, in this overall approach to overcoming some of our transportation problems in northern Canada is an error.
I do not think it is expounding any far-fetched dream to say that Edmonton will some day become the gateway to the north, for that is an established fact today. The province of Alberta accounts for about 27 per cent of western Canada's personal income, 28 per cent of its population, 33 per cent of its net value of production, 32 per cent of total private and public investment, and 49 per cent of its mineral production. In terms of future potential of resource development and industrialization, Edmonton is

indeed the hub of industrial activity. Edmonton is the fastest growing city in Canada. It is the provincial capital and the largest city in Alberta.
In assessing his transportation policy as it relates to northwestern Canada, I hope the Minister of Transport will reconsider the importance that the city of Edmonton and the province of Alberta will play in the development of an over-all policy. I know that we in the west are vitally concerned about the transportation needs of this country. We are very much aware of the need for improving our transportation services to the north. I hope that in the over-all assessment the minister is now undertaking, this matter will be taken into consideration, so that the north will grow in co-ordination with the facilities we presently have in Alberta, and in so doing create a much better system for all modes of transport.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to respond to this motion I will be directing my remarks principally to the observations made by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), the mover of the motion. In listening to him, I was interested to hear an expose of the ultimate almost in pure socialist doctrine. It was pure in the sense that it was theoretically doctrinaire. However, it was inpure in that it was disguised. One heard none of the slogans or none rather of the usual terminology which is employed in putting forward these claims; but nevertheless the underlying philosophy was the same. It appears to be based on the premise that nobody can accomplish anything or more particularly that no one can do anything as well as governments. I shall say a few more words about this later on. But quite clearly, the criticisms as outlined in the motion itself of government policy and its record with regard to Crown corporations can have been made only because of lack of knowledge. The government has, in fact, been most creative in developing new Crown corporations and in modifying the purposes of existing corporations which have both economic and social purposes. If I may, I should like to lay before the House a brief outline of policy developments in recent years. Then, I wish to go on to give a few examples of the very considerable achievements of Crown corporations in recent years.
In part of his peroration the hon. member for York South called for "more public involvement and public
March 23, 1973

investment". One measure of this involvement, of course, is investment itself. Let us take a quick look at the record. The most recent published public accounts, those for the year 1971-72, showed the total of government advances, loans and investments in Crown corporations stood at $11,998 million on March 31, 1972, almost $12 billion in advances, loans and investments in Crown corporations. This compares with an amount of only $4,468 million of $41 billion ten years before and with about $8 billion as of March 31, 1968.
We thus have seen a 50 per cent increase in the government's net investment-I emphasize net investment-in the last five years and more than a 250 per cent investment in the last ten years. I stress that this is a net investment since each year the government receives repayments on earlier loans and each year makes new loans. Yet, over the years in question the investment has grown after repayment in this very striking way.
Another measure of such involvement is legislative activity. I would like now to spend a few moments on that topic. As hon. members will see, the government has been very active in establishing new corporations and in adapting existing ones to meet a wide range of special needs. In the period from 1963 to 1972, legislation was presented to create among others, the following new Crown corporations: in 1963, the Economic Council of Canada; in 1966, the Company of Young Canadians; in 1966, the National Arts Centre; in 1967, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation; in 1967, the Canadian Film Development Corporation; in 1967, the Cape Breton Development Corporation; in 1967, the National Museum of Canada; in 1969, the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation; in 1970, the Canadian Salt Fish Corporation; in 1972, the Pilotage Authorities, the Atlantic, Laurentian, Great Lakes and Pacific; and in 1972, Uranium Canada Limited.
I shall have time later to mention only some of the accomplishments of some of these new corporations in their early years, but I ask hon. members at this time to note the names on this list. They will then appreciate, I am sure, that the government has had the insight to see the Crown corporation not just as a device with application in the economic sphere. They will note that this list includes new ventures in the social and cultural spheres as well. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the criticism contained in the resolution alleging a lack of public involvement has no foundation whatsoever in fact.
In addition to legislation establishing new corporations, there has been much legislation to expand and modify the powers of Crown corporations to fill the changing demands of the area they were set up to serve. For instance, in 1964, 1968, 1969 and 1972 legislation was brought in to affect the operations and powers of the Farm Credit Corporation, one of some age and reputation, to allow it to provide credit to groups of three or more farmers. The amendment to provide the Farm Machinery Syndicates Act and to raise the maximum on loans from $20,000 to $40,000 was brought in in 1964, to $80,000 in 1968, and to $100,000 in 1972. The amendment to allow loans to farming corporations and Indians farming on reserves was introduced in 1968.
Crown Corporations
No one could be unaware of the legislative initiatives which have so greatly increased the capabilities of CMHC in adding to and improving the housing stock available to Canadians. In 1964, long term, low interest loans to nonprofit organizations were made possible for the provision of low income rental accommodation, especially for elderly persons. In 1966, the National Housing Act was broadened to provide NHA financing for existing housing generally. In 1967, to stimulate private lenders support for housing, the formula was revised by which the maximum interest rate on NHA loans is established. Together with concurrent amendments to the Bank Act, this change spurred a return to the mortgage market by chartered banks. In 1973, extensive amendments to the NHA were introduced to the House of Commons in Bill C-135. These relate to government goals in the fields of low income housing, neighbourhood improvement, land assembly, new communities, and consumer protection, and also in 1973, the residential mortgage financing act was introduced to create the federal mortgage exchange corporation, a new Crown corporation, in order to provide additional financing mechanisms and institutions for the residential mortgage market in Canada.
The motion sponsored by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), in addition to dealing with Crown corporations in general, made allusions to two specific topics, namely, that the government had given preferential treatment to private corporations in the field of public transportation, and that the government had divested itself of certain holdings. I expect that my colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), will examine specifically the alleged criticism in relation to the field of public transportation. I, myself, would like to deal briefly with the complaint made by the hon. member for York South that the government had, if not committed, at least aided and abetted in some general and sinister disservice to the public of Canada by setting up the Canada Development Corporation and then proceeding to encourage its growth and effectiveness.
The hon. member for York South in his peroration exhorted the House to take heed and to avoid a sell-out of Canada. He was rather eloquent on this and indicated that one of the tasks facing Canadians in general and the House in particular was to avoid a sell-out of Canada. He indicated in some way that the establishment of the Canada Development Corporation was such a sell-out. If one has reference to the purpose of the Canada Development Corporation, which does not seem to have been very well understood, it is to:
help develop and maintain strong Canadian controlled and managed corporations in the private sector of the economy and will give Canadians greater opportunities to invest and participate in the economic development of Canada.
So that the purpose for which the Canada Development Corporation was established clearly was to avoid a sellout of Canada or Canadian resources.

For this, what is needed is a training ground for organizational and entrepreneurial talent in the private sector.
Hitherto the only training grounds, the only areas in which these kinds of skills could be obtained were the other multinational corporations, foreign owned and consequently foreign controlled. I think most Canadians would agree that the time was overdue when this kind of industrial organization should be not only possible for Canadians but practicable for Canadians. It would seem to be the case that the private sector neither had the resources nor the willingness to do this, so the stimulus was provided and the seeds were sown by the government through the agency of a Crown corporation, incidentally another Crown corporation, known as the Canada Development Corporation.
This is a corporation wholly owned by the Crown. All of its shares are owned by the Crown. All of its funding is derived from the Crown. The Crown already had under its control and ownership another corporation known as Polymer.

The object of the CDC is to develop the possibilities for a Canadian-owned, a Canadian-controlled corporation to acquire the size, the expertise, the technical know-how to compete effectively in a world dominated to a large degree by multinational corporations. In order to do this, to create such an instrument, it must have tools. Obviously, one of the tools is the Polymer Corporation. With a view to developing this, and to making it grow, it was transferred to the CDC.
There have been a number of suggestions made by the hon. member for York South that in his mind corporations are basically some form of ecclesiastical benefice which the government hands out to individuals or groups of individuals, with a view to making a profit. Apparently this is his vision of the airlines in Canada. According to the hon. member, one should not allocate an area or a route to Canadian Pacific Airlines rather than Air Canada because what is being allocated, to use the vernacular parlance, is gravy, or the gravy train, and if anybody is going to get the gravy train it should be the publicly owned rather than the privately owned airline.

I suggest that the purpose of Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines is the provision of air services to the Canadian public, and the question in one's mind should be: How can this service be provided most effectively and most efficiently to the public, not an enquiry into who is being granted a favour?
And by looking at it in terms of regarding all corporate activity as a source of money and nothing else, I think the perception of business organization by some hon. members tends to get a little distorted. One must look at the purposes of the CDC. I have already outlined them. I repeat that the purpose of the CDC is to develop an environment in which Canadians, as Canadians, can acquire the skills and the abilities in a practical way to have Canadian control and ownership of our larger resources, in the form of a multinational corporation operating on the world scene. This is not merely an endeavour, as the hon. member for York South would represent, on the part of the government to confer public benefits on a particular group for their enrichment.
The purpose of the Canada Development Corporation has to be considered and one can question whether it is achieving this. If the sole purpose of the CDC is, as alleged, merely to make a profit, then a lot of confusion will result, as it has, in the mind of the hon. member for York South. If the CDC is successful, as I suggest it will be, then it will be possible for Canadians to participate directly not only in the control, which is perhaps partly more properly a function of government in a regulatory sense, but also in the benefits inherent in ownership in their national resources which all too frequently tend to be in the hands of non-Canadians. One should, therefore,

support the growth and the success and the future of the Canadian Development Corporation.
In the field of plastics and synthetics in which Polymer has been engaged with a high degree of success for a number of years, there is now the possibility of expansion with the existence of the larger resources of the Canadian Development Corporation. In order to get into the field of pharmacology, the Canadian Development Corporation has acquired Connaught Laboratories in Toronto, with a view to expanding and making it a Canadian controlled operation in the pharmaceutical field.
In the House this morning, the hon. member for York South raised the question of whether the Canadian Development Corporation was contemplating the acquisition of the government's share of Panarctic Oils. This is an organization which, under Canadian control, is engaged in the development of oil and gas deposits in the high Arctic. I am persuaded that most Canadian resources would be brought to assist in this peculiarly and almost unique Canadian endeavour in oil and gas exploration. Everyone, including the hon. member for York South, takes exception to the fact that the bulk of the exploration and development of oil and gas resources in Canada is being done by large corporations which are, in corporate terms, both owned and controlled by non-Canadians. Here is a possibility of an organization which by its charter is now and will be Canadian owned and controlled, moving into and establishing a unique and entirely Canadian presence in this field. This should be welcomed rather than decried.
I think that the hon. gentleman from York South would welcome a Crown corporation wholly owned by the government doing this, although I am not too sure that members of the other party feel that the government should be in anything, and that perhaps Panarctic should be allowed to continue on its own. I welcome the notion that it is possible to bring greater resources to bear on this development through the mechanism of a Canadian controlled operation such as the Canadian Development Corporation setting out to accomplish the very purpose for which it was set up. The criticism, if any, of this is that it must continue to be owned by the government. The hon. member for York South assumes that the government can run things better than the private sector. Mr. Speaker, earlier today we heard from the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) who was not very complimentary to the CPR. Frankly, many times members of this party are not too complimentary either, but I would say to him, through you, Mr. Speaker, that if we did not have Canadian Pacific Airlines flying into Ottawa, transportation to this city would become a horror show. Air Canada does not seem to want to look after people coming to the capital city unless it suits it.
Having talked to many people in the air travel business, I am well aware of the high-handed attitude of Air Canada. This has been brought out in questions addressed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) in this House in connection with the price of air charters. In the travel field, it is necessary to have private competition in order to drive down and keep down prices, while at the same time giving the service that Canadians require.
In his speech, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) has advised this House that the government now has $11.9 billion invested in Crown corporations. I wonder if any investor ever invested so much money and received so little return. A great deal has been said about Crown corporations, but surely the reason for the Canadian Development Corporation cannot be solely its use as an executive school to train people for executive jobs. If that corporation is to have any validity, surely it should be out developing Canada, making it possible for Canadians to own Canada and helping Canada to go forward as a nation.
Mr. Speaker, I want to apologize to you for a question I put to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) two days ago when I asked him whether there was any justification for the sale to the Canadian Development Corporation of Polymer at $42 million less than the book value. Since that time I have had occasion to examine the balance sheets of Polymer Corporation going back for a number of years, and I have determined that in the last balance sheet that is available to the members of the House the difference is not $42 million but $55 million. The book value of Polymer, at the close of business on December 31, was $117,801,000. This corporation was sold for $62 million. I intend to go into that matter later this afternoon.
I want to make it clear that my party is not opposed to Crown corporations or public corporations. Nevertheless, the activities involving CDC and Polymer Corporation are a sorry mess. This must be brought to the attention of the House and of the people of Canada. When I say that my party is not opposed to the development of Crown corporations, let me remind you, Sir, and the members of the House, that it was my party which created the Hydroelectric Power Commission of Ontario, and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is my party that is prepared to examine priorities in Canada and, if necessary, but only if necessary, to create a Crown corporation to do a job that Canadians think should be done. Let me say this, as well. It will be my party that will look every day at Crown corporations and make sure they are doing their jobs. If necessary, we will institute reforms, to make sure that the sorts of things which have happened in the last

little while between Polymer and Canadian Development Corporation do not continue to happen in the public service.
I referred earlier to the financial statement of Polymer Corporation and the consolidated balance sheet of December 31, 1971. I say that we should have available the December 31, 1972 statement. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you will realize why we have not received it. I intend to comment on that as well.
In the statement of February 11, 1972 for the period ending December 31, 1971, the shareholders' equity in the corporation, that being the value accruing to the people of Canada, as asserted by the Auditor General and by Peat, Marwick, Mitchell and Co., chartered accounts, was $117,801,000. This corporation, belonging to the people of Canada, was sold to Canada Development Corporation for $62 million. Normally when you look at a balance sheet, you look for the assets of a corporation. This corporation has been operating since the early 1950's.

I am unhappy that the hon. member for York South sometimes referred to as the deputy leader of this government, is not here. He knows quite a bit about corporate balance sheets. In the normal course, if a company such as Polymer were put on the market, it would not be sold for its book value; it would be sold for many times book value. It would be sold on the basis of asset value, its prospects and productivity. But, the corporation in question was sold for $55 million less than its book value on December 31, 1971.
May I refer hon. members of the House to section 39 of the Canada Development Corporation Act, which provides that the governor in council may sell or cause to be sold a corporation at such fair and reasonable price as may be agreed upon. It lists Polymer Corporation and two or three other corporations. When we asked the President of the Treasury Board about this matter which was raised in the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee, we learned that a certain amount of departmental analysis had been done with respect to Polymer Corporation, and that the department had brought in a private appraiser. You may remember, Mr. Speaker, that when I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about this the other day, he said that he would look into this private evaluation, and per-

haps he would table it but perhaps he would not. We have looked into this question and found that a profit analysis was done. We are wondering about this. What kind of game is being played?
Is this corporation worth only $62 million? Because, if this is all it is worth, then annual report after annual report filed in this House, audited reports, press releases and fancy annual returns which have indicated the great profitability of Polymer Corporation, are not correct. If this corporation, Mr. Speaker, was worth only $62 million, it is clear that this House, this country and all of us have been lied to for years and years. This is what the Prime Minister says; this is what the President of the Treasury Board now says. He says we have been lied to. It was only worth $62 million all along. The $92 million worth of fixed assets in lands and buildings which the corporation owned, according to the audited statement presented to this House, do not mean a thing. The fact that the shareholders' equity was $117,800,000 does not mean a thing. The corporation was only worth $62 million.
One begins to wonder at the figures connected with the alteration in the price of that corporation. This was a cute deal. It provides that the price can go up if the performance of Polymer in 1973 and 1974 is satisfactory. And how do the people involved measure that performance? First, those involved in this deal suggest that companies are now being valued at four times earnings. Everybody knows, Mr. Speaker, that every corporation, even a poorly organized corporation, even Bell Telephone, is valued at about ten times earnings. Corporations that are involved in research and development are usually valued at close to 20 times earnings. But this corporation sold for a fair and reasonable price in accordance with the statutes of this country, is valued at four times earnings. The price may go up $10 million if the company earns $2.5 million after taxes in the years mentioned. Mr. Speaker, there is something rotten here.
I wonder what this government has to hide. We know, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) has had the financial statement of the Polymer Corporation since early February. What does he want to do with it? He wants to hide it. He does not want to show it. He is afraid to bring it forth.

We have to look into the game that is being played with the Canada Development Corporation. It is quite a game. The reason for the Canada Development Corporation is clear. It is a method of having a public corporation that does not have to report to parliament and, therefore, the people of Canada. That can be the only raison d'etre for this enormous fiasco.
What happened? We had a member of the board of the Canada Development Corporation buy another company, Venturetek. Did we worry about the price-earning ratios there? Did we worry about the asset values in the Venturetek deal? No. As a matter of fact, we put $4.5 million into Venturetek without any indication of possible profitability. Did we have proper appraisals of fair and reasonable prices for Venturetek or were they the same kind of fair and reasonable prices that were paid for Polymer? It does not appear that way to this side. Of course, the government may have the answers. The government should present those answers to this House. The government has all sorts of opportunities to do that, but they do not because this is a game. There is something hidden here and that is what we are concerned about.
I want to mention the Connaught Laboratory purchase. That was a good purchase, but after all, that lab was owned by the University of Toronto. Perhaps all we should have done was to have made a grant to the university for work. We just have the assimilation of another public corporation which has gone behind the Canada Development Corporation for perhaps no other purpose than to hide the activities of it.
If we are going to have public corporations, they must be accountable to parliament. We have had too much of this hanky-panky; too many buried statements and no answers. Possibly the idea was to sell Polymer to the Canada Development Corporation to sweeten the pot and bury some of their bad mistakes so that when the shares of the Canada Development Corporation are put on the market the corporation will have a balance sheet to talk about. Surely, public corporations must be accountable to parliament and parliament has to see what is there. I am sure my friends to the left will agree with that.
We have to develop a new industrial strategy for this country. That does not necessarily mean that the corporations which are part of that strategy must be public corporations. This party believes in private enterprise. This party believes it is the duty of the government to make the best possible climate for business, the growth of business and the growth of individuality within our nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate on the motion introduced by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) with a great deal of pleasure, especially after hearing the remarks of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury). I had to think of his official title because, when I closed my eyes and listened to him, I thought he was addressing the members as though he was addressing a meeting of the board of directors of the Power Corporation of Canada. I never heard such an outlandish sell-out as we heard from the minister today. It was absolutely incredible the way he talked about what should happen to public corporations in their relations with the Canada Development Corporation. In fact, he said those corporations which are owned by the entire population of Canada would be turned over to the Canada Development Corporation, and a select few investors would then have de facto control over those corporations. That is what I wish to speak on today.
The bill establishing the Canada Development Corporation was discussed in the House in 1971. It was a notoriously bad bill from its inception. The Liberal majority pushed the legislation through. The New Democratic Party was opposed. During the proceedings, NDP members presented several amendments, but to no avail. Some of them were very interesting. For instance, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) wanted the corporation to be a crown corporation directly responsible to parliament through a ministry so that this corporation might serve the Canadian people. Needless to say, when the amendment came to a vote, the Tories joined their Liberal friends on this issue and defeated this sensible amendment. The old line parties again stuck together to make the Canada Development Corporation entirely ineffective.
The hon. member for Waterloo made one final pitch, proposing that the word "company" be replaced by "Canadian nation", signifying that this celebrated corporation should serve the Canadian people. And, of course, again the friends of the corporations, the Liberals and the Tories, joined hands to defeat the amendment. The immense difficulty with the present Canada Development Corporation lies in the fact that it proposes to use public funds without any control by the taxpayers of Canada, through a responsible federal minister to parliament. On top of that, the legislation establishing the corporation allows it to acquire control of already existing crown corporations. In other words, what is in public hands in Canada-and that is not very much-can pass to private profiteers disguised by the glorious name of the Canada Development Corporation. As the best outline of that methodology we had the speech by the President of the Treasury Board to this House today. In terms of the interests of the people of Canada, that speech was outrageous.
Who is running this so-called Canada Development Corporation? Again I refer to the NDP objections made in this House of Commons on December 29, 1971, by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who
 moved a motion that the directors of the CDC divest themselves of their directorships in private corporations. Needless to say the hon. member's motion was defeated. Here are some of the reasons it was defeated. Who are the directors of the Canada Development Corporation? Let us begin with the chairman, Mr. H. A. Hampson, former director of Laurentide Corporation-some people call them "loan sharks"-of Capital Dynamics Management and of the Power Corporation of Canada; I repeat, the Power Corporation of Canada. Of course, Mr. Hampson divested himself of these interests, but let us remember that his friends remained behind to ensure that business would keep booming in case there should be an eventual return to his former position.
Another director is Mr. Louis Desmarais, who is also a director of Canada Steamship Lines, Davie Shipbuilding and Blue Bonnets Raceway. His brother of greater fame if the Desmarais who is a member of the board of directors of the Power Corporation of Canada. Lately little brother has joined big brother on the board of directors of the Power Corporation of Canada. Then we have Mr. F. H. Sherman, well connected with the Bank of Nova Scotia, Dofasco and Polymer. Dofasco is the corporation which lately has been running ads over the radio saying they have a wonderful relationship with the government, that they take one of their employees, show him how government works and then they take him back. I wonder what kind of information he takes back with him. Then there is Mr. H. H. McCain, chief owner of McCain Foods Limited and half a dozen subsidiaries struggling hard to replace the Irving family as the barons of New Brunswick. These are all members of the board of directors of the Canada Development Corporation.
There is one more, who may seem a relatively innocent member of the board of directors of the Canada Development Corporation, a Mrs. L. Thtir, vice-rector of the University of Quebec. You may assume that this is a sort of token representative from the academic community; but if you check into it, Mr. Speaker, you will find that she happens to be a director of Bell Canada, that profit-tapping corporation which profits from operating telephone lines in Canada. Let us not speak of her marital connection with Mr. Thtir, who is none other than a former member of the Economic Council of Canada and presently holds a senior position in the Department of Finance.
I will name one more individual, Douglas Kendall. He has had fairly good connections. He was once with Hermes Electronics and de Havilland Aircraft, but more remarkably is a former executive officer with Venturetek, now derected by his impoverished son. Last fall the Canada Development Corporation invested $4.5 million in Vanturetek. Legally speaking it was an investment by the CDC and, I am sure, not a family self-help project from a good father to a delighted son. There may have been some other assistance provided through this great venture by the board of directors of the CDC because Mr. Tony Hampson, chairman of the board, undoubtedly agreed to that transaction. He is a good friend of Mr. Kendall senior and has been from the time they served on the General Adjustment and Assistance Board.
When this issue arose during the election our leader, the hon. member for York South, raised hell, as he should.
March 23, 1973

Even the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) got into the act and said that CDC operations should be suspended. But he failed to remember that the Tory party joined with the old-line party across the way to defeat every substantive amendment moved by this party to put teeth into the CDC and turn it into a true Crown corporation that would buy Canada back. Hon. members seem to forget that.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the CDC needs capital. The $250 million given to it by the federal government would not go far enough. They need capital to invest in companies in which the CDC directors at least have a sentimental interest. Where do you get the capital that is needed? From the prosperous Crown corporations. CDC has already gulped up Polymer, though I hope parliament will have the last say on that matter, as well as on the CDC's intention to get the 45 per cent federal interest in Panarctic. We heard the President of the Treasury Board outline the method to be used, which I find outrageous. Then from Panarctic we can move to the idea of swallowing up Eldorado Mines and other public corporations. So we have the basic situation that companies are being taken from the people of Canada, turned over to the CDC and passed into the hands of vested interests; let there be no mistake about that.
We in the NDP are not interested in giving away the little public holdings that we do have to a dubious Canada Development Corporation where public interest may be reduced to a mere 10 mer cent of the shares. We want to keep the Crown corporations that we have, and indeed we want to see more of them. Let there be no mistaking where this party stands on that issue.
During my introductory remarks I mentioned several names and several corporations which are linked directly and sometimes indirectly, with the Canada Development Corporation. I wish I had time to establish a more complete picture, but to be brief all I have to say is that in the time of Caesar all roads led to Rome. In the time of Trudeau all roads lead to the Power Corporation of Canada.
What is the Power Corporation of Canada? It is a rather intimate club of Canadian businessmen who obviously decided to get some extra cash from a small investment. It is a holding corporation, so that they do not have to pay income tax. Let me restate that: They have to pay a little income tax. In 1966 they contributed to the welfare of Canada a total of $48,000 in the form of income tax on profits in the previous five years of $62.3 million. Mr. Speaker, if only the ordinary taxpayer of Canada could get such a favourable income tax rate!
There is nothing illegal about this; it is simply the fact that the present tax laws of Canada as passed by the Liberal party and supported by the Tory party as represented by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the former financial critic of that party, allow a corporation such as the Power Corporation of Canada, that great friend of the Liberal party, to get a corporate rip-off the extent of which the Canadian people have never seen before.
Crown Corporations
Mr. Speaker, I assure the House that the corporation is a club of somebody's. It has its claws all over the place. It has related directorships with all kinds of federal bodies such as the Bank of Canada, the DREE advisory board, the advisory board to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, GATT, and of course the Canada Development Corporation. If I had more time I would reconstitute the cobweb in which the spider is the Power Corporation of Canada. Instead, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to bear with me and allow me to table in this House of Commons a little chart which I drew up in my spare time after the general election. It is an outline of the corporate welfare state in Canada and all its complications in respect of that great protector, the Liberal party, with the Power Corporation in the middle and the advisory boards all around it. Mr. Speaker, perhaps you would give a ruling on whether I may table this chart.

What we know for certain is that Mr. R. G. I do not have a single quote from the Tory bagman, but please not the press statement by the Leader of the Official Opposition a few days ago on the position of the Tory party in respect of the corporate rip-off. A few days ago he made a grandiose speech in Regina saying that those who voted for the New Democrats were sold out by the New Democrats. Then he comes back to Ottawa and makes another grandiose speech saying, "Well, we cannot really hurt our corporate friends, can we, now?" The official version of the happy association of the federal government with its corporate masters reads like a dream. It is a gentleman's agreement. On December 29, 1971, the then minister of finance, Mr. Benson, innocently told the House of Commons:
