speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always sorry to see such important matters dealt with so quickly. I am not blaming anyone; I know that we are all under pressure and do not have enough time to prepare speeches that might be of great use in giving a direction to Canadian politics.
Mr. Speaker, the motion of the New Democratic Party reads as follows:

That this House regrets the failure of the government to develop policies to create and operate Crown corporations for the benefit of the public, and condemns the government for divesting itself of its holdings and giving preferential treatment to private corporations in the field of public transportation to the detriment of corporations which belong to the people of Canada.

There can be no doubt that this motion involves some extremely serious principles. There is a whole philosophy to be examined, but, unfortunately, I see this problem brought down to a few specific cases or incidents, or to matters that have nothing to do with Crown corporations.
I am sorry to have missed this morning's speech by my hon. colleague, the member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski); unfortunately, I had a delegation in my office and was unable to be in the House. I am sorry because I should have liked to know the points of view of all the parties, although I suppose I shall hear them in due course.
I should therefore like to speak on this subject at a level that will, I hope, clarify the debate, and also to explain at least my position, if not necessarily that of the government on this basic problem of the relations of Crown corporations with the government and with private enterprise.
Why are Crown corporations created, Mr. Speaker? It is not because there were socialist governments in Canada, but simply because one day, for one reason or another, the state felt it had to set up an institution to safeguard the interest of the public at a time when no private corporation was interested in establishing that institution, or the nature or purpose of that institution was so closely related to public interest that we could not leave that institution in private hands.
Why, for example, was Air Canada created? The founder of Air Canada, if my memory serves me well, was the Right Hon. C. D. Howe and his socialist tendencies were very limited. He certainly did not do it because he felt aviation should be controlled by the state but undoubtedly because he saw that aviation was developing at a very rapid pace in the world and no private corporation wanted to run the risks; so a Crown corporation was created which was called Trans-Canada Air Lines.
Let us review the history of Crown corporations. Why was Polymer Corporation created? It is not because C. D. Howe had turned socialist but because nobody wanted to invest large amounts of money in a new product. If I remember well, it was synthetic rubber at the time of the war and that is how the government of Canada created Polymer Corporation.
March 23, 1973

I think it would be useful at this time to recall what some people had to say to remind us of the principles underlying the establishment of certain Crown corporations as well as some minor but very interesting contradictions in the history of our Crown corporation.
Lord Morrison of Lambeth gave this definition of a Crown corporation:
If we establish the public corporation, it must be for certain reasons. What are they? They are that we seek to combine the principle of public accountability, of a consciousness on the part of the undertaking that it is working for the nation and not for sectional interests, with the liveliness, initiative, and a considerable degree of the freedom of a quick moving and progressive business enterprise. Either that is the case for the public corporation, or there is no case at all.
A Conservative member said in the House in 1949, and this may be referred to by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House:
The official opposition-
Which was Conservative at that time.
-does not believe in Crown corporations. We think that is one method of getting away from control by parliament.
This member was, a few years later, a member of the Diefenbaker cabinet which was responsible for the creation of an entirely new Crown corporation, the Canadian World Exhibition Corporation, and for a large increase in the operations of a number of Crown corporations, including the one that provoked the speech just quoted and was accused by the now official opposition of frustrating the efforts of parliament to exercise control. The same administration was accused of "doing its best to tear down the Crown corporations of the country".
Although the majority of Crown corporations were set up under Liberal governments, Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Bank of Canada and the Canadian Wheat Board were in origin creations of Conservative governments.

So there was no particular principle underlying the creation of those corporations. Indeed, if we consider their background, we will recognize that they are not based on any given philosophy. Their founders have acknowledged just the same that public interest was at stake and that some institutions had to be created to protect it.
Now, to deal a little closer with the subject which I want to discuss, I will say that if public interest was involved and that a corporation was developed thanks to the money of Canadian citizens who financed it, who made good its deficits and provided some capital, this corporation could not be considered as a private enterprise. It deserves special protection because it specifically exists to uphold and protect the public interest.
People may complain that we are using public funds, but why for example did private enterprise not provide the millions of dollars required when Air Canada was created? Because it was too risky as indeed it was to produce synthetic rubber.
Crown Corporations
We know that transportation, especially air transportation, is now vitally important for all countries, particularly for Canada. Why? Our country being so big and having so little population, it would be appreciably weakened if we did not have a rapid air transportation system. Furthermore, I think Canada could not exist today without fast communications in the east, west, north and south and the only way to achieve this end is to have aircraft- jet aircraft.
As it happens, there are more than two companies operating in this field, that is CP Air and Air Canada. We also have regional carriers which as private enterprise are operating simultaneously with government corporations.
From the domestic point of view, I would not be against regional carriers. I think we need companies of lesser importance and in a better position to look after the more remote regions, whereas the larger companies are operating on a wider scale on medium and long trips. Therefore, I do not intend to criticize regional carriers.
Can a government monopoly be dangerous on the international level? I would say since it cannot even exist. International competition is between countries and not necessarily between two national companies. For instance, if there were only one intercontinental airline in Canada, it still would have to compete with Air France, BOAC, Sabena, Lufthansa and other companies.
Now, it so happens in Canada, and this is born out by history, that there are two companies: Air Canada and CP Air. CP Air was supposed to serve western Canada, Asia, Australia, Japan, Hong Kong and extend to that part of the world west of the Vancouver coast. Air Canada was supposed to serve the other part of the world; up to 1960, it had absolute monopoly on the main air routes in Canada.
Some guidelines have been established. One of them concerns domestic transport and a good case can be made for it. It is said that Air Canada should have at least 75 per cent of the Canadian market, while CP Air should get no more than 25 per cent of it. Predominance was to be preserved for Air Canada. This is true of the Canadian market, but not of the international market. In fact, from an international point of view, there are no limits, and unless the policy is well defined, the situation could be reversed, that is Air Canada could become eventually less important than CP Air. For instance, if the 800 million people of China were to start travelling tomorrow, the company would become a really important one.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that on this point, we have to be careful. In my opinion, Air Canada should remain the important company in Canada, and not only from a Canadian standpoint, but also from an international standpoint. It should remain our most important company and, on the other hand, it should not tolerate competition from another company on the same routes; CP Air having been given the right to serve Japan and China, if Air Canada is given the right to serve Hong Kong, even if it is claimed that they are not the same countries, this is competition, because CP Air serves Amsterdam and Air Canada serves London and Paris.

March 23, 1973
Crown Corporations

speechtext:
There are several, and very important ones at that!
I did not mention any "vast representation"; I referred to trade union representation and the member for Scarborough West should not make me waste one instant because he knows it is true. He knows that the trade unions are represented on the Economic Council of Canada. He also knows that the trade unions are represented on the Unemployment Insurance Commission Advisory Committee. He knows that the trade unions sit on all the advisory committees of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. The trade unions have been represented in all commercial delegations. A former vicepresident of the Labour Congress of Canada could supply the list.
I do not mean that capitalists have no influence in Canada, they do have influence and we agree on this but so have the trade unions. This was not my point. The point is to know whether the private sector wields sufficient influence to have the government decide in its favour regardless of the common good and this is the area to be discussed. Everyone knows that private enterprise has the upper hand in Canada. Everyone knows that, including the NDP governments elected in British Columbia, in Manitoba or in Saskatchewan. The premiers of those provinces have stated publicly that they are not against private enterprise. They fear they might lose a vote. The hon. leader of the NDP stated: I do not want to be a doctrinaire. I agree with him and I would have said the same thing. However, let nobody come and tell me that we created the capitalistic private enterprise. It was there! It is there as well for Mr. Schreyer, Mr. Barrett and Mr. Blakeney. Of course, "they play ball with them". However, these governments manage so that private decisions affect government decisions as little as possible. That is where the problem lies.
Instead of telling us that capitalists are represented on committees, perhaps it would be better to find out cases where decisions have been affected by the presence of these people, at the expense of public interest. That is the point which I am concerned about. Everything else is but "electoral chit-chat".
Mr. Speaker, I am not allergic to Crown corporations; I am rather for them. For instance, the Northern Transportation Company Ltd. has developed the Mackenzie area up to the Arctic; not one private business had dared to make investments in northern transportation, because it was not profitable. Therefore, a very efficient corporation was created which assists us in developing the Canadian North. This corporation belongs to the people of Canada and must be protected in order to meet its obligations. Of course, it must be efficient. Certainly it is so. When companies are not efficient, the government is not interested in protecting them and then, there is a very easy procedure: management must be changed.
For instance, the National Harbours Board has played and continues to play a very important part in the growth
March 23, 1973

of our country's economy. Harbours are institutions of public interest. There are private habours but they are of no public importance. Who has taken the necessary steps to move the grain? Who takes care of port facilities for containerized shipping? It's the National Harbours Board.
The St. Lawrence Seaway Authority is also a Crown corporation. Nobody would have paid hundreds of millions of dollars to open up that seaway, to promote trading with the Great Lakes area and the United States and to link central Canada with the Atlantic.
Mr. Speaker, a company set up in such circumstances deserves to be protected to the extent that it is efficient and performs its duties.
Now there is the whole field of railways: the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. That is probably the main subject of any debate dealing with transport. Here again, I believe the opposition should tell us about its policy positions. Should a company like the Canadian National, for instance, be exclusively profit-oriented? I say no, Mr. Speaker. I say that the Canadian National should be efficient, should conduct research, should try to be forward-looking in railway transportation. Only the Canadian National, like any Canadian railway company, has a public responsibility. Consequently, it often has to provide service at a loss in certain areas. And that is part of our concept of transportation in Canada and gives us an idea of what a Crown corporation should be.
If railway companies keep on abandoning so-called uneconomic services, a day will come when there will be trains only in Montreal and Toronto, because those are the only two cities with enough population to make railways economic, which makes no sense at all. Since certain institutions have a public duty to perform, they must assume directly or through the government financial responsibilities that a private company surely could not take on.

If only you had resisted the temptation two minutes more, I could have finished my remarks, Mr. Speaker.
I merely want to add that it is certainly not the opinion of most Canadians that our corporations should be nationalized just for the fun of it, that smoothly running corporations, not state-owned, making normal profits and developing normally should be transformed into Crown corporations. I believe no one, even those who claim to be socialists, would call for nationalization of all our corporations. I have never heard such a contention brought
Crown Corporations
forward, even by NDP members, since the CCC manifesto in Regina.
However, I feel that an economy such as ours calls for a certain number of government corporations, occupying a privileged place and, although they are functioning properly, allowed by the government to perform the tasks they were created for. They must be efficient. Obviously, if a bureaucracy forms in these corporations and cannot be dislodged, there must be means of changing it and renewing the management. We have our philosophy on this, Mr. Speaker. If private enterprise goes in where it thinks it can make money, it does so at its own risk. But in the government sector, we must safeguard the public interest.
There is, however, one slight distinction that remains to be made, and I shall finish on this, Mr. Speaker. I am not saying that private interest automatically and necessarily overlooks the public interest, but simply that that is not its prime concern. Its first concern is to make a profit, after which it can start to take account of other values such as the public interest. It is the other way round for a Crown corporation: its first concern is the public interest, but at the same time it must try to be efficient and economically viable, to show that people can act on motives other than profit. It can also act to be of service to the public. Such, Mr. Speaker, is the aim that I set myself with regard to the Crown corporations under my administration. I shall not try to weaken them. On the contrary, I am going to try to make them stronger and more efficient and to do what I can to make them give better service to the public of Canada.

I am nevertheless encouraged, because the minister has suggested that the Crown corporation I am going to criticize was created expressly to protect the interests of the Canadian public and to serve it.
I simply seek the protection of a certain sector of the public-that which I represent-and I want it to go on getting the service it needs.

I welcome this oDportunity, Mr. Sneaker, to address parliament about Crown corporations and service to the public because it gives me the means of registering a public protest against the failure of one of our Crown corporations to provide the full service expected by members of the community-

speechtext:
As I was saying, it gives me the means to protest against the failure of one of our Crown corporations to provide the service expected by members of the community which I have the honour to represent in company with my colleague the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon).

March 23, 1973
Crown Corporations
My argument is to the effect that just by being a public or a Crown corporation does not make the enterprise faultless or white and pure. However, before getting to that matter I should like to say a word or two about the motion itself. The initiators of this motion are taking aim at private corporations and are, I suggest, intent on promoting the notion that all corporate activity and enterprise in this country should be nationalized.
In the same breath that they use to advocate this socializing theory, they protest violently against big, monopolistic corporations. Monopolistic monoliths, Mr. Speaker, are creatures of man that all too readily can become monsters whether they be private or public, nationalized corporations. Nationalized monopolies can be just as great a menace and can disregard the public interest just as conclusively and effectively as a monopolistic private enterprise. They can be just as difficult to move.
It is my personal conviction, after examining all the evidence, that as a general proposition the public interest is best served by competition and that competition can be between private and public companies or between private and socialized companies, although I do not see competition between socialized companies and nationalized companies.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) and his colleague in the New Democratic Party suggested that the nationalized corporation is the good guy and the private corporation the bad guy. Let me give the House just one instance of how the good guy can get at the throat of the bad guy, all in the knowledge that any shortfall the good guy may suffer will be made up by a generous parliament, which in the end means the generous public, the public of Canada.
Let me detail what is happening in my area. My colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), has spoken of the dangers of a monopoly public utility failing to give service. Here is an instance. An island people is heavily reliant on transport, not just to receive all it needs and to ship excess goods to market but also to maintain personal touch with the mainland. Our island, Vancouver Island, is no exception. We have our commercial and personal needs to be fulfilled. Developments are in train, however, that cause us grave misgivings. These developments are in the hands of the government, or a government agency, to control. I suggest, in fact, that too little is being done to safeguard the requirements of the population of Vancouver Island.
For over one month I have been trying to get satisfaction from one or other of the articulations of the minister's department. I am referring to a scheme I have heard about to reduce air service facilities between the island and the mainland. Let me give you the following by way of background, Mr. Speaker. The last ferry leaves the Saanich peninsula for the mainland at nine o'clock p.m. Travel time from shore to shore is one hour and 20 minutes. The last flight at present leaves Victoria airport for Vancouver airport at 23.35. Travel time, airport to airport, is 20 minutes. The first ferry leaves the island for the mainland at seven o'clock in the morning. The first air service now leaves Victoria airport for the mainland at
[Mr. Munro (Esquimalt-Saanich).J
five minutes after seven. That is Air Canada flight 170; and I am not making a commercial, as you will soon appreciate.
Thus, as things now stand, between half past eleven at night and seven in the morning there is no way of getting to the mainland. To parody the comment, "the continent is cut off," made in Britain whenever fog closes in and disrupts flights and sailings to France, Belgium and other places, we do not want to isolate the mainland, Mr. Speaker: we like to preserve contact with the mainland. Seriously, however, we may need, early any morning, to get to the mainland for reasons of business, family matters, illness, and so on.
The seven o'clock flight is a good one. It is operated by Air Canada, a publicly-owned corporation, and has been well patronized. I am told by a reliable informant that the flight carries on the average between 35 and 40 passengers daily and the aircraft has a full load seating capacity of about 48 passengers. As I say, it is a well patronized service. Now we hear that Air Canada is threatening to eliminate that service. This is the public utility so highly praised by hon. members to my left. As at the end of April, that service may well disappear, to the detriment of the inhabitants of the island who for one valid reason or another may want to go over early to the mainland.
I have been doing what I can to ensure that this service continues. At first I got in touch with Air Canada. The service is not being eliminated, I was told; it will be supplied by the flight of another airline scheduled to leave at 8.15, one hour and 15 minutes later. That service, moreover, at present is already well booked. However Air Canada might wish to describe it, that existing service will be dropped if present plans are carried through. As Air Canada now sees it, there will be no flight from Victoria to Vancouver until 8.15.
I next appealed to the Canadian Transport Commission. To this plea I have so far had no response, which makes me wonder how the CTC operates as a regulatory body. Is it responsible for ensuring that service to the public is maintained? I regret very much that the minister is no longer present. I hope he will read my questions in Hansard and will in due course reply. Has that commission any regulatory control over schedules? I feel I am entitled to know this and the population of the island is entitled to know it. And if it does not have this regulatory power, where do I turn to ensure that the mainland's isolation is not prolonged unduly each morning and does not extend beyond the present seven and a half to eight hours?
What are some of the other consequences of dropping this service? Many Vancouver islanders have business or even tourist's interests in the east and overseas. What results will they feel from the elimination of flight 170 from Victoria which leaves at seven o'clock? Well may I ask that question. I have looked at the air schedule. At present, if a passenger leaves on that flight from Victoria he can, should he so desire, catch the following eastbound flights from Vancouver to Toronto, Ottawa or Montreal.
There are two CPA flights leaving Vancouver at 8.35 and nine o'clock respectively, and an Air Canada flight leaving at 8.20. By being unable to leave Victoria on that early flight, the passenger would obviously miss the first of these; he could not get away from the island until 8.15
March 23, 1973

and he would miss the CPA flight leaving Vancouver at
8.35.	He might miss the second CPA flight at nine o'clock because of delays involved in transferring from one flight to another, in offloading luggage, and so on. He would miss the Air Canada flight that is most convenient for me, the one that comes straight to Ottawa. Having been made to miss two CPA flights and one Air Canada flight, he would be forced to wait for the Air Canada flight which does not leave until 9.15.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), in fact all ministers and most executives these days, claim that they want to maintain the widest possible range of options. Why should executives, even backbench executives in the opposition, have their options reduced? I say the flight at seven o'clock from the island ought to be maintained. If I, for example, were able to catch the flight at 8.35 operated by CP Air from Vancouver, I could be in Ottawa at half past four. Unless I spend the night, at some cost, in Vancouver waiting for the 8.15 flight from Victoria, I will be forced to catch the 9.15 flight leaving Vancouver and I would not get here until half past six, one hour and a half later. I like the options the way they were. Surely Air Canada should be required to serve the public need: it is a national, public utility as we heard eloquently expressed in this House today and it should not be permitted to eliminate a well patronized scheduled flight from the island.
But that is not all, Mr. Speaker. What about travellers going in other directions? Remember, arrival in Vancouver by the early flight is 7.25 at present. If that service is eliminated, it will not be possible to get to Vancouver until
8.35.	As well, there are departures for Mexico in the morning, by that villain CP Air. One flight leaves at 7.45. You might just catch it if you left Victoria at seven o'clock. Or you may have to wait until the next flight at 2.30 in the afternoon. You may wish to go to Hawaii or the South Pacific. If so, departure time is 8.30. If you leave the island at seven o'clock you can catch that flight. If you must wait until 8.15 you would miss it, and there is not another flight until the next day. Of course, the flights to the South Pacific are all operated by Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
I am wondering if it is not possible to draw certain inferences from these considerations. I submit that there is room in all this to infer that Canada's national public carrier is not serving the national interest-I hope the proponents of nationalization are listening-at my end of the country inasmuch as it is not fulfilling the requirement to provide a much needed service. The 8.15 service, incidentally, is not to be provided by a public service but by another private service, Pacific Western, the airline which was mentioned this morning by my colleague from Vegreville. The first Air Canada flight to Vancouver will not be in the air until 10.30. I think this is deplorable. If this is public service, I think I will opt for private service. That sort of performance is unacceptable to those whom I represent on southern Vancouver Island. If Air Canada is a public service in the true sense of the word, it ought to provide the service needed by the public in the area in which it is operating. It will be obvious from the foregoing, Mr. Speaker, that I disagree with the initiators of this motion on certain aspects of the matter which they are putting forward. Nationalized monopolies, as I think I
Crown Corporations
have shown, are not my bag. We are heading for trouble if we head in that direction, as has been suggested.
I share the misgivings that hon. members have expressed with respect to Polymer and with respect to the government's policies affecting that corporation. I am particularly disturbed to see Polymer disappear. I have a soft spot in my heart for Polymer, because Polymer gave me my Master's degree by providing me with an early model of Crown corporations on which I could base my Master's thesis. The concept was a good one, although it could be improved. However, it was an enterprise that ought to have been confined to specific areas of activity and allowed to occupy a monopolistic position only in special circumstances, such as the wartime emergency situation which gave birth to Polymer when the need for rubber was absolutely essential.
Many are the failures of this government which we on this side of the House regret. Many of its policies we condemn. Among them is its failure to bring forward to this House measures that will halt inflation and reduce unemployment. In the context of this motion, we condemn not only the government on these grounds but for having divested itself of its holdings in Polymer. Even more, Mr. Speaker, we condemn the government for the way in which they have done this, by refusing to give a proper accounting to this House which created Polymer in 1940 or 1941 and which was once headed by a frontbencher on the other side of the House. There was no annual report, no profit and loss statement and no statement of assets and liabilities at the time of sale. Talk about questionable practices, Mr. Speaker, when one public corporation ingests another without let or hindrance-by Your Honour's leave, I avoid some forms of language

and without a report after the event except by an entry in the estimates! We have reached the stage of monogopoly, where one monopoly gulps up another. We have come, indeed, to a sorry pass. I sometimes think of that concept of life when I try to work out what happens when a snake consumes itself from its tail. What happens when it starts to swallow its stomach?
I will go along the road of condemnation with the NDP that far, the road which we have been invited to take, the road of condemning the government on the manner of its handling Polymer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform the House of events that led to the sale of Polymer Corporation Limited to the Canada Development Corporation and summarize the role played by the Minister of Supply and Services in accordance with his responsibilities as the minister responsible for Polymer Corporation Limited up to the point of sale. Parliament approved in principle the sale of Polymer Corporation Limited to the Canada Development Corporation by virtue of section 39(1) of the Canada Development Corporation Act, which provides:
The Governor in Council may sell or cause to be sold to the company, at such fair and reasonable price as may be agreed upon by the Governor in Council and the company, the whole or any part of the capital stock of any or all of the following:
(a)	Polymer Corporation Limited;

March 23, 1973
Crown Corporations
(b)	Eldorado Nuclear Limited;
(c)	Panarctic Oils Ltd., and
(d)	Northern Transportation Company Limited but subject, in the case of the capital stock of Panarctic Oils Ltd., to any agreements relating to the sale of capital stock held by the Crown.
The Canada Development Corporation Act became effective November 18, 1971. Subsequently, the government authorized the Minister of Supply and Services to undertake negotiations with the Canada Development Corporation for the sale of Polymer Corporation. The following considerations were taken into account in pursuing the sale of the company. The original rationale for the existence of Polymer as a domestic producer of a strategic material in a national defence context no longer existed. We must remember that the government's objective in establishing Polymer Corporation in May of 1942 was to remedy a shortage of natural rubber as a strategic wartime material. However, for some years it has appeared that this need is no longer evident. In fact, Polymer evolved into a multinational producer-marketer. It had been profitable over the years, but profits had been subject to fairly wide swings and at the time of sale were on the decline.
To protect its earnings base, the company sought to diversify into non-rubber lines. This diversification and the large capital requirements that it entailed could best be met by a change in ownership which would provide for access to private financing and freedom of business choice. The vehicle best suited for providing immediate response to its capital needs and ensuring that the benefits of ownership continue to accrue to all Canadians had already been envisaged by parliament when the Canada Development Corporation was created.
On the other hand, if Polymer had not been sold and had continued as essentially a synthetic rubber business rather than allowed to diversify, it would likely have ceased to be a profitable business, being faced with an increasingly competitive situation and higher raw material costs. It would, therefore, have become a charge upon the public treasury, which would not have been in the best interest of Canadian taxpayers. Again, if Polymer had not been sold, but allowed to diversify, Polymer could have been placed in direct competition with a range of Canadian enterprises in the private sector; and the government did not feel that it should become involved in a host of varied enterprises such as building materials, soft drinks, snowmobiles or even underwear, for that matter.
Taking all of these factors into consideration, it then seemed desirable to proceed with the sale. The remaining question was one of arriving at a fair and reasonable price to both parties. The negotiated price which was agreed upon was arrived at with reference to several valuations, one of which had been provided by the firm of Wood Gundy Limited. Terms and conditions of the sale included the payment of $62 million in the form of Canada Development Corporation shares, and a formula whereby the government of Canada will share in 1973 and 1974 earnings over a certain level of rubber, latex and plastics up to an additional payment of $10 million.
The government approved the sale on July 27, 1972, which is contained in the relevant order in council PC 1972-1715 of that date. The sale became effective July 31,

1972, and subsequently the shares held by the Minister of Supply and Services were delivered to the Canada Development Corporation upon payment of $62 million in the form of Canada Development Corporation shares. Accordingly, the responsibilities of the Minister of Supply and Services as minister responsible for Polymer Corporation ceased as of July 31, 1972, the effective date of sale.
It is my considered opinion that the decision to sell Polymer is a valid one, that the price arrived at was fair and reasonable based on the best information available at the time, and that the method of conducting the sale was correct. Furthermore, I am convinced that with the active support of the Canadian Development Corporation, Polymer will be provided with a flexible and businesslike framework in the profitable pursuit of its objectives as a Canadian-based multinational company. It also seems to me that the acquisition of an experienced and reputable organization such as Polymer will provide the Canadian Development Corporation with a cornerstone to pursue its own investment strategy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by giving the House a little information that I have been able to gather since the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) spoke just a few minutes ago on the question of labour representation on various advisory bodies or boards of directors of Crown corporations in this country. I do not want to try to put words into his mouth by suggesting he was saying that there were large numbers of labour people on these bodies, but at the same time he certainly left the impression that there were considerable numbers of labour people on them. I for one, as well as many other people in this country, would like to challenge this view, because it is very apparent that where there is labour representation it is very much of a token nature. I have before me this afternoon very few documents but I thought by reading from them I might help set part of the record straight. If the Minister of Transport wishes to complete the record at some other time, I invite him to do so.
I have a list of the directors of Polymer Corporation. There are ten directors. Of these ten directors there is one who comes from the labour movement. Indeed, broadly speaking we could say that there is only one person who comes from the community at large; the rest of the directors, of course, are from the corporate community.
With regard to the Canada Development Corporation, the list discloses 21 directors. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) entertained the House a while ago with their background, so I shall not do the same. I simply say that of those 21 directors there is one from the labour movement. If this is representation, I call it token representation.
I have gone back over the list of directors of Polymer Corporation since 1948, and a few years ago the case was not the same at all. There were no representatives from the labour movement or community at large on the board of directors of such corporations, particularly this one. It is nice to know that there has been a change of heart. We realize that there are such things as legitimate labour unions in this country which have the right to be repre-
March 23, 1973

sented on boards of directors and advisory councils of various enterprises run directly or indirectly by this government and parliament.
Where before there were none, we now have one representative out of ten, one out of 20, one out of 18-token representation. It is highly reminiscent of what happened a number of years ago when we in North America watched television ads that in most cases were produced in the United States and failed to see at any time a black person taking part in a television commercial. Over the past three or four years there has been a change of heart and we have come to admit in North America that black people do live here. In order to bend to this change of heart, the commercial interests in this country now every once in a while play black people in commercials in recognition that they form part of our population.
The same approach of tokenism is used on boards of directors of publicly-owned corporations in this country. I am not talking at the moment about privately-owned corporations: I am sure it is a rare case indeed when a privately-owned corporation gets someone from the union to sit on its board. I am talking about publicly-owned corporations and advisory bodies set up by and for this parliament.
These remarks are not going to be the burden of my address this afternoon, if I can call it an address. I want to address myself to the whole question of the motion that is before the House, a motion that can be paraphrased in cruder language as the sell-out of the public of Canada's interests to the private corporate interests of this country.
In the past we have had reason to be proud of our crown corporations. Indeed, if you go back, Mr. Speaker, over the history of reports that have come to this parliament from, for example, Polymer Corporation, there is a note of constant and well deserved pride in the success, prosperity and usefulness of a Crown corporation such as Polymer. I have taken the time to go back over reports across the years but I will not read extensively from them. Let me simply say that we have in the Library of Parliament a bound volume of reports issued by Polymer Corporation.
It touches one's heart a little when one looks at some of the earlier reports. For example, the report to the minister of reconstruction and supply for the 12-month period ending March 31, 1948, is typewritten. How humble, how spartan; but at the same time, how complete! Reading through the report you get more than pictures; you get more than general statements. You get accurate descriptions of the goings on and procedures of the corporation. As a matter of fact, the more you move forward through the history of the corporation, the glossier the documents get and the vaguer they become. I do not want to be very conservative in my attitudes, but it is sometimes worth while to go back to a simpler, more direct world, a world where you can find information that is more complete than is the case now, with all the help and advice our various corporations receive from various PR flaks.
About two and a half years ago there was a sudden creation by fiat of a rather large category of persons in this country. Overnight, a large section of our population became the bleeding hearts of Canada. The bleeding hearts of Canada were said to have very little power, and
Crown Corporations
indeed they have very little power. But they have some power of comment. I am told by the National Association of Bleeding Hearts that some time last year they thought they would state their presence in this country by offering a medal, an order so to speak, which they called the Order of the Lily Liver. They were bound to offer the Order of the Lily Liver to the government of the day. It was awarded for its daring, perhaps what we would call its temerity, its bravery in taking an idea such as the idea of the Canada Development Corporation, which was supposed to be the medium through which the people of Canada would have gained, first of all, some control and power over the corporate processes of this country and begun to regain Canadian control over the industry and economy of Canada.
What is the first thing that the Canada Development Corporation does? It takes over a corporation that is already fully Canadian and fully owned by the people of Canada-Polymer Corporation. As a second step in its temerity and bravery, what does it do? It takes over Connaught Laboratories, another entity completely in the public realm owned by the University of Toronto, in effect owned by the public of Canada. It was a truly Canadian corporation. It was a very valuable corporation which had an international reputation. This laboratory provided a service not only to Canadians but to people throughout the world through its research in drugs and the provision of inexpensive drugs to hospitals and other institutions in this country. So after taking over Connaught Laboratories, the National Association of Bleeding Hearts decided to give the Order of the Lily Liver, with bar, to the Canada Development Corporation. What they were in effect trying to say was that the original idea had been completely reversed and that the Canada Development Corporation as set up in late 1971 was not the ideal which had been held up for the people of this country to watch and to hope for.
We have had some reference this afternoon to the past, to the days of C. D. Howe. I was walking behind the East Block today at noon when I happened to walk behind the bronze statute of our fifteenth prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King. He has his hands stuck behind his back. I would almost swear that his fingers were crossed. I thought they were crossed because he was afraid the great spirit of C. D. Howe would storm this Hill today to tell Liberal members of the front benches that they were completely betraying his ideas and his work. In the past, the CCF were not necessarily the great friend of C. D. Howe, but certainly they admired his forthrightness, his energy and his dedication to building Canada. I am sure that if he were to come back today, Mackenzie King in bronze image would have a great deal of reason to cross his fingers, because there would be some mighty scolding of the people who now sit on the front benches.
The Canada Development Corporation can now extend its bravery and take over Panarctic. Perhaps it could take over Eldorado. But before this happens let us stop to consider what we are up to in the ventures of the Canada Development Corporation. The story behind the Crown corporation is that it was to give to the people of Canada some degree of control over their economic destiny. It was

March 23, 1973
Crown Corporations
not simply, as has been mentioned in the House this afternoon, to do a job where private interests could not do it: there was something positive in the idea of the Crown corporation which I believe has been completely lost from sight.
Rather than taking over Panarctic and putting it into the hands of CDC which would some day, I am sure, sell it to the private interests of our country, this parliament should take steps to instruct the government to have Panarctic become really and truly controlled by the Canadian people. At the very least we should have 51 per cent control of this enterprise. This enterprise will be a major factor in the exploitation and development of our oil resource in the northland. Surely when it comes to this very scarce and important resource, we want it completely under Canadian control.
When it comes to Eldorado, before we begin handing over Eldorado to the Canada Development Corporation perhaps we should begin by giving it the same treatment that was given to Denison Mines. A few years ago the owner, the president of Denison Mines, threatened to shut down the mine because he could not sell its uranium. An agreement was struck between Denison Mines and the Government of Canada on December 23, 1970, which in effect subsidized Denison Mines to the tune of $29.5 million to cover three-quarters of the cost of uranium stockpiling. The president of Denison Mines, Mr. Roman, had the ingratitude some time afterward to state that he was having a hard time because he had to pay out $6 million or $7 million in losses over the stockpiling. He had the further ingratitude of biting the hand that fed him, or of trying to bite the hand that fed him, by running in the following election.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: How much did he spend on that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
A mere $90,000, a figure for which C. D. Howe would not have had a measurement. But if we can help Denison Mines to that extent, surely we should pay some concern to Eldorado which has received no such subsidy, is now working below capacity and over the past number of months has been forced to lay off workers.
In the time I have left I should like to talk about Polymer more specifically, because it has been the object of concern over the past few days, as it well ought to be. There is an old Latin saying-I do not know whether Latin is an official language in this House or in this country-caveat emptor, "Let the buyer beware". In this case the saying should be transformed so that it would be caveat vendor, "Let the seller beware". We, the people of Canada, are the people who are selling Polymer Corporation to the Canada Development Corporation and we should beware in respect of the details of the transaction.
This House has been informed this afternoon of certain figures relating to the value of Polymer. I would like to give some more figures of that value. We know that over the years the net assets of Polymer have far exceeded, year by year, the paltry sum which is being offered for it by the Canada Development Corporation. Net assets, less liabilities, for the year 1971 were $163 million. For the year 1970 they were $163 million, for 1969 they were $160 million, and for 1968 they were $155 million. Going away

back to the year 1962, the value of the net assets, less liabilities, was $90 million. So even in 1962 it was worth more than the sum now being offered for it in CDC shares. Note that it is in shares, and not dollars. Judging from some of the plans which are being put forward for CDC, we might have a right to question the value of these shares in the future. So we as the vendors certainly ought to beware.
Let us look at the book figures. We know that in the world of corporate transactions, book figures are only part of the picture. There are other ways to calculate the value of Polymer. I need not repeat now that the sale price is between $62 million and $72 million, depending upon the profitability and earnings of Polymer in the next while. But let us look at more effective estimates. There could be three methods of calculating the value of Polymer. We might take the estimated consolidated book value on December 31, 1972, which is $128 million. Then we could add to this the estimated excess depreciation because over the years, of course, Polymer has depreciated its machinery, stock, and so on, and some of this machinery in terms of book value has a zero value although the machinery is still working and is still being used. The machinery still has a value. Everybody in the industrial world knows that you can have a piece of machinery which is totally depreciated, in so far as tax purposes are concerned, while the machinery is still operating, still cranking away and still producing and making very good use of itself.
Method A is that you estimate the consolidated book value as at December 31, 1972, add the estimated excess depreciation and arrive at a figure of $163 million-a cool $101 million above the $62 million. Method B is more commonly used to evaluate corporations and companies. You take the company projection of average earnings, after taxes, for 1973-76, which would be about $16 million, and multiply it by the capitalization factor, discounting growth by 100 per cent, which yields roughly 7 per cent after tax. This is a very conservative set of figures and multipliers. Multiply the effect 14 times. I am striking a middle figure here because we know, as the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) said a while ago, that ten times is the minimum factor and we know that in the petroleum and petrochemical industry 22 times is the more reasonable figure. So I will take 14 times. That gives you the method B valuation of $224 million. Subtract $62 million from that and you will see that the people of Canada might be losing.
To be even less conservative and go the full range of valuation as it might be carried on in the petrochemical industry, let us use a factor of 22, which is not common. You will have a figure which certainly skyrockets beyond the 14 times, giving you much more than the $224 million valuation for the company I mentioned earlier. So there is a very real and serious gap between the value of this company and the money that has been paid for it.
If it were the case that it was solely a book transfer between a Crown corporation and the Canada Development Corporation which was totally in public hands, then we could say that this is just a matter of a book entry. But it is not so. The Canada Development Corporation will be
March 23, 1973

putting out shares to the public. And let us not kid ourselves: when we talk about the public we do not talk about Mrs. MacGillivray with a few dollars in her socks; we are talking about people who have the money to invest in the stockmarkets of this country, and that is a limited number of people. We are not talking about people so much as about other corporations, other companies or other institutions. So here we have the possibility of a Canadian Crown corporation being effectively sold for peanuts to the private interests of this country. No wonder that the great spirit of C. D. Howe might shake itself a little on a day like this and come roaring up to this parliament to scold the Liberal frontbenchers.
There are other questions which are involved. They relate to the presentation of the financial report of Polymer. I have gone back over a few years to find out when the financial reports were presented, and I have the dates: 1971, February 11; 1970, February 12; 1965, February 11; |960, February 21; 1959, February 5. It is now March 23. Indeed, if I may quote the immortal words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), "it's spring". Winter has gone by, the winter of our discontent has gone by, and according to the normal pattern we should have a report on this very large and important Crown corporation because there are questions at least, to be asked. Accusations have been made about the Crown corporations which ought to be cleared up fully.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: There are questions to be answered, too.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to cite from an Associated Press report which originated in Geneva and reads as follows:
The International Federation of Chemical and General Workers ... said Polisar International SA-
That is the international trading company of Polymer.
-which has an agreement on technology exchange with the Soviet state committee for science and technology, also integrates international cash flows and profits "to minimize taxes and accumulate investment capital for further expansion overseas."
What could be behind this? We all have an idea of how multinational corporations can operate through processes of invoicing so that they can minimize their tax burden. A multinational corporation operating in Canada and producing goods in Canada could be, in effect, selling goods directly to Arkansas through Belgium and therefore, when it invoiced Belgium for a figure less than what they would be invoicing Arkansas, foresaw that the profit made in Canada was small but the profit made in Belgium was large; but it so happens that the tax grab in Belgium is smaller.
It is known that the tax levels in Switzerland are indeed modest; they run at approximately 8 per cent. They even beat us in this country when it comes to letting off the corporations. What we want to see in this parliament is the financial report so we can go into it thoroughly to see what the international trading practices of Polymer have been, because certainly it has been doing business with Polisar, its own subsidiary in Switzerland, and it would be very interesting to know how over the years Polymer has paid taxes effectively to Switzerland which could have been paid to the people of Canada.
Crown Corporations
Of course, in the past, we did not mind that the directors of Polymer used every legal means at their disposal to reduce the tax burden on Polymer because, after all, we the people of Canada were still the owners of Polymer; so whether we got it in taxes or profits, we still had it. But now the problem is that this company has been sold out and we will be losing out on the back taxes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been pleased in today's debate to hear the various arguments put forward-most of which, incidentally, I agree with-concerning the contemptuous action taken by the government with respect to the Polymer and CDC deal. The previous speaker stated in his final remarks how deplorable it was that we have not as yet been given the right to look at Polymer's last annual report.
I feel his comments are particularly appropriate when we bear in mind that up until yesterday we were debating in the House Bill C-133. During that debate I pointed out that I found it was strange that this government would come to parliament and request an increase in the ceiling for CMHC so that it could borrow up to $10 billion, and that they would request the ceiling with respect to the amount of mortgage investment they could insure should be increased to $19 billion; yet they had not given the House the courtesy of presenting to the House the most recent annual statement for CMHC which should have been presented for year ended December 31, 1972.1 pointed out that in both respects, the amount of mortgage investment that had been insured and the actual amount of loans advanced to that corporation were significantly lower than their existing ceilings.
I am indeed very surprised, startled and annoyed to be now presented, the day after the debate, with the annual statement for CMHC, bearing in mind that that statement, I suggest, had been deliberately withheld from the House until the bill was passed in principle last night. I would call the attention of the House to the fact that a review of the figures with respect to CMHC reveal all too well why the Trudeau government did not dare introduce that statement prior to the passage of the bill in principle. The fact is CMHC profits have again tumbled. This is the third year in a row that that corporation has borrowed more from the treasury, has increased their assets, has increased their number of employees, but has made less money.
Let me give you the figures, Mr. Speaker. Based on borrowings from the Government of Canada which we find total, as of the end of 1972, $6,166,000,000 compared with borrowings the previous year of $5,600,000,000, we now find that the corporation's after-tax income is $3,182,000 compared with $7,432,000 the year before. Surely that is a significant factor that the House should have been aware of prior to our being asked to give second reading to Bill C-133.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when we are considering the desirability of Crown corporations we should

March 23, 1973
Crown Corporations
keep in mind that, while it may be necessary to have certain Crown corporations for certain services, wherever possible Crown corporations should be divested and put back into the private sector. Let me contrast, for example, the picture in Canada with respect to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the comparable company in the United States which, incidentally, used to be state-owned and which is referred to as the Federal National Mortgage Association. I would point out that that corporation, which is only three times the size of our Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has had a sensational growth in profits, 686 per cent in fact, which is due largely to the fact that the American authorities worked out an ingenious plan for returning that corporation back into the private sector.
At the present time on a board of 15, 10 of the board are nominated by the stockholders at large of the corporation. Those stockholders are made up largely of those who use the services of what is called Fannie Mae. I would point out that the company is, first of all, neither a purely private enterprise nor a purely governmental agency but, rather, is a combination of the two. It is ultimately controlled by the President of the United States and it is also charged with the major responsibilities of implementing U.S. housing policies. It is expected to seek profits for its stockholders-I would emphasize that because to me profit is simply the evidence of efficiency. If you do not make profit, in all likelihood it indicates bad, sloppy management.
Fannie Mae is oriented to make profit for the stockholders. It has been renamed once, it has been restructured three times and its mission has been refined and redefined twice. This is something that is long overdue with respect to CMHC. That is a corporation which was set up for one purpose, and rather than being redefined in order to be able to properly cope with the existing problems in Canada, it has been allowed to stay in a stratified, immobile condition; and judging from the current financial statement it is not even serving the government or the people of Canada properly.
In the United States, Fannie Mae has as a principal goal or mission the provision of money to builders and lenders at the most reasonable terms. It services, in short, the savings and loan associations, the banks and insurance companies in that country. I think it is interesting to note that it not only insures mortgages-and this is a recent diversion-but it has gone into the conventional mortgage field in an extremely aggressive way, becoming in effect a type of mortgage exchange where people can buy and sell mortgages of a conventional nature in the United States.
Fannie Mae has risen to her present pre-eminence among mortgage lenders because she managed, in some respects, to escape from federal authorities. In short, she escaped from Basford-type domination. As a government agency, created in 1938, that corporation naturally found it easy to borrow money in the private market to make mortgage loans. I would point out that in our stultified approach to CMHC our government has never, even to this date, allowed CMHC to go into the private sector and raise money.
It takes the easy way out, and that is simply to go to the Minister of Finance and ask for another $100 million or $1

billion, as we have been requested in this House, or perhaps $2 billion and we give them another $2 billion of loaning authority. I emphasize that the comparable company in the United States does not depend on the federal treasury to the extent that CMHC does in this country. The comparable company there is privately financed both as to equity and as to debt.
I would also mention that in order to keep its funds in the black, it has become completely free of government restraints with respect to debt limits. This has put it in the position where, unlike our CMHC which is included in the gross liabilities of Canada, it does not have to be included in calculating the gross liabilities of that country. I would also like to mention that in May, 1970, control of the company's board of directors moved into the hands of some 14,800 private stockholders. The stock, in fact, is now traded on the New York Stock Exchange and has been one of the sensations on that exchange. Its profit and its growth have been so sensational that the public have bought the stock and it has risen from about $5 in 1968 to a current price of over $20. In fact, at one time it went over $25, a fourfold to fivefold increase with respect to that stock.
The profits in that corporation at the present time are running at about $70 million. Imagine! Here is a corporation, privately oriented, that I would suggest is doing an even better job in its field than the comparable company in Canada. It is only three times the size of our corporation, yet it is earning in the area of $70 million compared with our corporation earning $3 million. This is something that those who have such a fondness for Crown corporations should bear in mind. The fact is, government ownership is not the most efficient way to get the proper efficiency in a corporation.
The stockholders in Fannie Mae elect ten of the directors and the President of the United States appoints the other five. The charter granted to the company by the U.S. Congress gives George Romney, as Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, "general regulatory powers" over Fannie Mae affairs, decisions involving dividends, stock issues, total debt and borrowing of money. But, and I would stress this, at all times the company is geared to a profit-making orientation.
I have drawn attention to these similarities or dissimilarities between the Canadian approach with respect to CMHC and the American approach with respect to Fannie Mae, not because I feel there is any particular merit in the U.S. corporation because it is American, but I am simply stating to this House that in considering the motion before us we should bear in mind that Crown corporations are not to be encouraged in further development or expansion. As this parliament progresses we will be able to demonstrate some completely irresponsible activities with respect to some of the Crown corporations that have been either administered, continued or in some cases spawned by the present government. This growth in Crown corporations is something that should be arrested at the earliest possible opportunity.
When we look at the returns produced by Crown corporations in this country, the results are startling. Their total
March 23, 1973

assets have grown from under $4 billion in 1962 to over $12 billion in 1972. Their earnings, if you pull out debt calculations and the earnings that they can make by the Bank of Canada, which is simply a bookkeeping entry, are something like $70 million. We are talking in some cases about the largest corporations in the land having assets in the aggregate of $12 billion, earning somewhere around $70 million in the aggregate. Some of these corporations in fact have been in a deficit position; yet we find that there is an encouragement, a propensity on the part of the government to inflict still more Crown corporations upon the nation.
Mr. Speaker, I rose only to make a few comments because I feel it is a tragic thing that this country has been so inflicted under the Trudeau government, and I sincerely hope that there will be a trend away from loving Crown corporations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE INTERESTS OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see by the clock that I have only five minutes, so I will not be able to go into the details of the speech that I had prepared. I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), who preceded me, in regard to the value of Crown corporations. I believe this typifies the mythology about free enterprise and how it has been the great salvation of the country in the past and will be in the future. Perhaps the hon. gentleman should look at Canadian history and realize that it is a myth to say that this country was developed solely by free enterprise. Let us remember that the great economic ventures in this country were joint ventures between government and the private sector. We find something that seems to be typical of the Canadian businessman, that he lacks the financial wherewithal and the audacity or courage to take risk ventures.
I refer the hon. gentleman to the development of the Canadian Pacific Railway, that great band of steel which united this country from east to west. Was that solely a private enterprise undertaking? We find out that the private enterprisers came crying to the government that they could not make it on their own and needed help, so the taxpayers provided the CPR, that private corporation, with $25 million-that was not peanuts in those days- with 25 million acres of land, and a guarantee that they would face no competition for 25 years. We begin, then, to see in the development of the Canadian economy a partnership between government and private enterprise.
Crown Corporations
The next great venture in the area of communications was Trans-Canada Airlines. No businessman was interested in developing a national airways, so the Canadian government undertook to develop it for the Canadian people. We have been served very well by Air Canada, despite this government's attempts to undermine it by giving lucrative routes to Canadian Pacific Air lines.
Many unprofitable, small railway systems in Canada were going out of business, which would have deprived the people of northern Ontario and other areas of service. The government decided that service should come before profit, so it took over the railways and amalgamated them with the Canadian National Railways' system, incurring a huge debt but not giving up. The CNR is running efficiently today and making a profit, notwithstanding the fact that it has the huge debt of the private system hanging over it.
Let us not be carried away by the myth that free enterprise alone developed this country. Free enterprise has caused a huge amount of foreign investment in this country to the point where over 60 per cent of the manufacturing is foreign-owned, over 82 per cent of oil and gas wells are foreign-owned, and 99.9 per cent of the petroleum industry is foreign-owned. If we rely solely on foreign private investment, this country will cease to exist in the near future. What we need is a Canadian Development Corporation, not of the sort the Liberal party has, but one that is truly owned by the public of Canada and truly designed to develop Canadian industry, to buy back some of the foreign-owned industry and not to buy up profitable public corporations such as Polymer, Eldorado, and so on.
I urge this House not to fall for this mythology propagated by many members of the Conservative party and many, but not all, of the Liberal party. We need a strong publicly-owned business system in this country. I am thinking of examples we have now. We need a very strong Canadian development corporation to keep Canada for the benefit of Canadians.
